name: Mobile Security
description: Security and privacy of Android and iOS apps, permissions, app stores, and mobile platforms.

uss.narrative:
The earliest listed work, from USENIX Security 2018, reflects a field maturing along two tracks: deep platform and analysis tooling, and privacy. On the systems side, "Charm: Facilitating Dynamic Analysis of Device Drivers of Mobile Systems" (USENIX 2018) and "ATtention Spanned: Comprehensive Vulnerability Analysis of AT Commands Within the Android Ecosystem" (USENIX 2018) pushed analysis down into drivers and modem interfaces, while "Tackling runtime-based obfuscation in Android with TIRO" (USENIX 2018) confronted malware that actively hid from analysis. In parallel, "FlowCog: Context-aware Semantics Extraction and Analysis of Information Flow Leaks in Android Apps" (USENIX 2018) and the meta-study "Discovering Flaws in Security-Focused Static Analysis Tools for Android using Systematic Mutation" (USENIX 2018) showed both the promise and the fragility of the static-analysis toolchain the community had come to rely on.

The next shift, around 2019-2020, was a turn toward privacy policy and data-flow accountability at app-store scale. "PolicyLint: Investigating Internal Privacy Policy Contradictions on Google Play" (USENIX 2019) introduced automated reasoning over the gap between what apps say and do, and "Actions Speak Louder than Words: Entity-Sensitive Privacy Policy and Data Flow Analysis with PoliCheck" (USENIX 2020) extended this to entity-sensitive flow checking, becoming a heavily cited anchor for policy-compliance research. The same period broadened the platform attack surface dramatically: "FIRMSCOPE" (USENIX 2020) mined pre-installed firmware apps for privilege escalation, "PARTEMU" (USENIX 2020) opened TrustZone software to dynamic analysis, and "FANS" (USENIX 2020) fuzzed Android native system services, signaling that vendor firmware, secure-world code, and system services were now first-class targets.

By 2021-2022 the area diversified into ecosystem and human-factors questions alongside novel side channels. Work like "An Investigation of the Android Kernel Patch Ecosystem" (USENIX 2021) and "Why Eve and Mallory Still Love Android: Revisiting TLS (In)Security in Android Applications" (USENIX 2021) revisited whether years of attention had actually fixed patching and TLS validation, while "A Large Scale Study of User Behavior, Expectations and Engagement with Android Permissions" (USENIX 2021) centered real users across countries. New attack classes appeared in third-party libraries ("Understanding Malicious Cross-library Data Harvesting on Android", USENIX 2021), app-in-app super-app ecosystems ("Identity Confusion in WebView-based Mobile App-in-app Ecosystems", USENIX 2022), and physical side channels ("Charger-Surfing", USENIX 2021). Voice assistants also became a recurring theme, from "SkillExplorer" (USENIX 2020) to "SkillDetective" (USENIX 2022).

Most recently, in 2023, the field is wrestling with machine learning robustness and entirely new sensing modalities. "Continuous Learning for Android Malware Detection" (USENIX 2023) tackles concept drift that erodes ML malware classifiers over time, a sign that detection itself is now a moving target. Meanwhile the definition of a mobile platform keeps expanding: "Going through the motions: AR/VR keylogging from user head motions" (USENIX 2023) treats AR/VR headsets as the next mobile frontier, and "Eavesdropping Mobile App Activity via Radio-Frequency Energy Harvesting" (USENIX 2023) shows app activity leaking through ambient RF, pushing mobile security well beyond the classic phone-app threat model.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this NDSS collection treats mobile security as an ecosystem problem rather than a single-app one. "Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators: A Global Study of the Mobile Tracking Ecosystem" (NDSS 2018) mapped how third-party services pervade apps worldwide, and companion 2018 papers looked inward at the platform itself: "AceDroid: Normalizing Diverse Android Access Control Checks for Inconsistency Detection" and "Resolving the Predicament of Android Custom Permissions" probed weaknesses in Android's access-control and permission model, while "Bug Fixes, Improvements, ... and Privacy Leaks" tracked how PII leakage evolves across app versions. The theme is a maturing platform whose own safeguards and third-party dependencies both need auditing.

By 2019-2020 the field broadened along two axes. One is new attack surfaces beyond app code: "Life after Speech Recognition" (NDSS 2019) fuzzed voice-assistant misinterpretation, "BadBluetooth" (NDSS 2019) weaponized malicious peripherals, and "Understanding Open Ports in Android Applications" (NDSS 2019) found listening services on the device. The other is measurement at the network and sensor level. "FlowPrint: Semi-Supervised Mobile-App Fingerprinting on Encrypted Network Traffic" (NDSS 2020) — the most-cited paper here — showed apps are identifiable even through encryption, and "Learning-based Practical Smartphone Eavesdropping with Built-in Accelerometer" (NDSS 2020) turned an innocuous motion sensor into a microphone, establishing sensor side channels as a durable concern.

Around 2021-2023 the work grew more regulatory and defensive. "PrivacyFlash Pro" (NDSS 2021) automated privacy-policy generation to meet legal requirements, "Understanding Worldwide Private Information Collection on Android" (NDSS 2021) quantified data harvesting globally, and "On the Insecurity of SMS One-Time Password Messages" (NDSS 2021) tied platform permissions to authentication failures. "Post-GDPR Threat Hunting on Android Phones" (NDSS 2023) then asked whether OS-level safeguards actually enforce the privacy rules regulators mandate — a shift from finding leaks to auditing the guarantees meant to stop them.

The most recent papers show the frontier moving to new platform layers and blended boundaries. Super-app ecosystems appear in "Understanding Miniapp Malware" (NDSS 2025) and "Better Safe than Sorry: Uncovering the Insecure Resource Management in App-in-App Cloud Services" (NDSS 2026), while "Automated Mass Malware Factory" (NDSS 2025) uses adversarial techniques to mass-produce Android malware. The 2026 work also revisits old problems with new lenses: "Cross-Boundary Mobile Tracking" dissects Java-to-JavaScript information diffusion in WebViews, "MVPNalyzer" audits mobile VPNs, "CHAMELEOSCAN" uses LLM-powered UI exploration to catch iOS chameleon apps, and side-channel and authentication research continues in "Side-channel Inference of User Activities in AR/VR Using GPU Profiling" and "Know Me by My Pulse" on wrist-worn PPG. Mobile security today spans hybrid app boundaries, mini-app platforms, wearables, and AR/VR — with LLMs increasingly on both the attack and defense sides.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work on this list, from IEEE S&P 2018, already staked out two enduring threads in mobile security. One was human and social: "The Spyware Used in Intimate Partner Violence" (S&P 2018) reframed the phone as a weapon that abusers turn against people close to them, rather than a target for distant hackers. The other was physical and technical: "Speechless: Analyzing the Threat to Speech Privacy from Smartphone Motion Sensors" (S&P 2018) and "EyeTell: Video-Assisted Touchscreen Keystroke Inference from Eye Movements" (S&P 2018) showed that a phone's own sensors leak what users say and type. Alongside these, "The Rise of the Citizen Developer" (S&P 2018) and "Mobile Application Web API Reconnaissance" (S&P 2018) began treating the app ecosystem and its cloud back-ends as a security problem in their own right.

Through 2019 and 2020 the field broadened along both lines. Sensor side channels matured into precise fingerprinting with "SensorID: Sensor Calibration Fingerprinting for Smartphones" (S&P 2019), which turned factory calibration quirks into a permission-free device identifier, while "Why Does Your Data Leak?" (S&P 2019) traced leaks into the cloud back-ends apps depend on. The interpersonal-abuse thread grew into a measurement discipline with "The Many Kinds of Creepware Used for Interpersonal Attacks" (S&P 2020). At the same time researchers dug beneath the app layer into the platform itself: "SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems" (S&P 2020) systematized the trusted-hardware foundations of mobile devices, and "An Analysis of Pre-installed Android Software" (S&P 2020) exposed the supply-chain risk baked in before a user ever installs anything.

The early 2020s sharpened the tooling and widened the lens. Analysis frameworks like "TextExerciser" (S&P 2020) and "ConDySTA" (S&P 2021) pushed dynamic and taint analysis further, while "Android Custom Permissions Demystified" (S&P 2021) and "How Did That Get In My Phone?" (S&P 2021) showed the permission model and app-distribution channels were still structurally weak. The community also grew more socially and globally aware, studying "Mobile Loan Apps in Kenya" (S&P 2022) and "Mobile Gambling Scams" (S&P 2022), even as classic side channels kept advancing through "AccEar" (S&P 2022) and BLE physical-layer location tracking (S&P 2022).

The most recent years show the frontier moving onto new hardware and new software stacks. The sensor-inference tradition jumped to immersive computing, from "Privacy Leakage via Unrestricted Motion-Position Sensors in the Age of Virtual Reality" (S&P 2023) to "Eyes on your Typing" (S&P 2025) and, in 2026, "EyeSpy: Inferring Eye Gaze via Side-Channel Attacks Against Foveated Rendering" and "When VR Meets BCI" (both S&P 2026). In parallel, on-device machine learning became its own battleground, from "ShadowNet" (S&P 2023) through "No Privacy Left Outside: On the (In-)Security of TEE-Shielded DNN Partition" (S&P 2024). The 2026 papers make clear where the area now stands: local LLMs on phones are the newest attack surface, whether recovered through memory forensics in "Recovering and Rehosting Mobile Local LLM Conversations and Contexts" or audited for privacy compliance in "Navigating Developers' Quagmire" (S&P 2026), while super-app platforms ("Convenience at a Cost") and contactless payment apps ("Secret State Leakage Attacks") extend the old ecosystem-and-TEE concerns into today's most complex mobile environments.

ccs.narrative:
Mobile security at CCS has covered the Android permission model, privacy leakage through apps and sensors, and biometric authentication. In 2018, the community examined how apps and browsers exploit mobile hardware: The Web's Sixth Sense: A Study of Scripts Accessing Smartphone Sensors (CCS 2018) showed web scripts abusing gyroscope and accelerometer data for fingerprinting, and PatternListener: Cracking Android Pattern Lock Using Acoustic Signals (CCS 2018) recovered unlock patterns from acoustic reflections. JN-SAF: Precise and Efficient NDK/JNI-aware Inter-language Static Analysis Framework for Security Vetting of Android Applications with Native Code (CCS 2018) tackled the hard problem of analyzing Java-native hybrid apps.

The 2019-2020 period brought intent and privacy-policy analysis. DeepIntent: Deep Icon-Behavior Learning for Detecting Intention-Behavior Discrepancy in Mobile Apps (CCS 2019) used icon-behavior associations to catch apps behaving contrary to their stated purpose, while Automatic Fingerprinting of Vulnerable BLE IoT Devices with Static UUIDs from Mobile Apps (CCS 2019) extended mobile analysis to the companion-app ecosystem. Enhancing State-of-the-art Classifiers with API Semantics to Detect Evolved Android Malware (CCS 2020) addressed classifier aging as malware evolves.

By 2021-2022, consistency checking between policy and behavior became standard. Consistency Analysis of Data-Usage Purposes in Mobile Apps (CCS 2021) automatically detected mismatches between declared data practices and actual runtime behavior. EchoHand: High Accuracy and Presentation Attack Resistant Hand Authentication on Commodity Mobile Devices (CCS 2022) pushed acoustic biometrics to commodity phone hardware with strong anti-spoofing guarantees.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this set treats the mobile app as a leaky container whose real risks come from what it quietly ships elsewhere. Large measurement studies mapped the scope: "Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators" (NDSS 2018) charted the global third-party tracking ecosystem, while "Bug Fixes, Improvements, ... and Privacy Leaks" (NDSS 2018) tracked how PII leaks changed across app versions over time. Alongside this, a wave of program-analysis papers tried to catch leaks in the code itself — "FlowCog" (USENIX 2018) and "Finding Clues for Your Secrets" (NDSS 2018) added context and learning to information-flow analysis, and "JN-SAF" (CCS 2018) extended vetting into native JNI code. A parallel and strikingly human strand appeared at S&P 2018 with "The Spyware Used in Intimate Partner Violence," which reframed mobile threats around abusers and stalkerware rather than faceless attackers.

Around 2019-2020 the field's center of gravity shifted from "is there a leak?" to "does the app's stated behavior match its real behavior?" "PolicyLint" (USENIX 2019) automated the reading of privacy policies and found internal contradictions, and "PoliCheck" (USENIX 2020) closed the loop by matching actual data flows against policy text on a per-recipient basis, with "Consistency Analysis of Data-Usage Purposes" (CCS 2021) pushing this into stated purposes. Two other durable threads consolidated here: encrypted-traffic analysis, where "FlowPrint" (NDSS 2020) showed apps stay fingerprintable even without payload access, and machine-learning malware detection, where "Enhancing State-of-the-art Classifiers with API Semantics" (CCS 2020) and "Structural Attack against Graph Based Android Malware Detection" (CCS 2021) grappled with evolving and adversarial malware. Platform-level and side-channel work rounded out the period, from "SoK: TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems" (S&P 2020) to accelerometer-based eavesdropping in "Learning-based Practical Smartphone Eavesdropping" (NDSS 2020), echoing the earlier "Speechless" and "PatternListener" sensor attacks of 2018.

By the mid-2020s the recurring lesson is that mobile defenses must keep moving, because both apps and attackers do. "Continuous Learning for Android Malware Detection" (USENIX 2023) made concept drift the explicit design target rather than an afterthought, treating detection as an ongoing process instead of a fixed model.

The most recent work shows the field expanding along two fronts at once: new platforms and LLM-powered analysis. The 2026 papers push into app-in-app and cross-boundary surfaces — "Cross-Boundary Mobile Tracking" (NDSS 2026) traces Java-to-JavaScript data diffusion in WebViews, "Better Safe than Sorry" (NDSS 2026) examines mini-app cloud services, and "MVPNalyzer" (NDSS 2026) audits mobile VPNs — while also reaching iOS, wearables, AR/VR, and EMV contactless payments. At the same time, large language models have become analysis tools: "CHAMELEOSCAN" (NDSS 2026) uses LLM-driven UI exploration to detect iOS chameleon apps, and "Navigating Developers' Quagmire" (S&P 2026) applies LLMs to SDK-level privacy compliance — a direct descendant of the PolicyLint/PoliCheck line, now automating the hardest reasoning about what third-party code really does.
